title: Hubble spies cosmic dust bunnies
caption: The giant elliptical galaxy NGC 1316 (Fornax A), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Fornax A, NGC 1316 · constellation Fornax · about 60 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: Ranked #25 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Surprisingly intricate loops and blobs of dust hide inside NGC 1316, a giant elliptical galaxy also known as Fornax A, about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Fornax. This Hubble image reveals its dust lanes and star clusters, tucked away like dust bunnies in the corners of a room.

That dust is a surprise. Elliptical galaxies are usually thought of as smooth collections of older stars, with little of the gas and dust that fill spiral galaxies. Finding such complex dust inside NGC 1316 therefore calls for an explanation.

The dust lanes and star clusters suggest one. They are evidence that the galaxy was built from a past merger of two gas-rich galaxies. The dust and clusters may be leftovers of that union, still visible long after the two became one.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.69 x 2.73 arcminutes) and distance (60 million light years), the frame spans roughly 47,000 × 48,000 light-years. Its light set out about 60 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures and Hubble's sharp view reveal dust lanes and clusters invisible to the eye.
